body:
Why different international agreements exist

Biotechnology creates different kinds of international concerns. Living modified organisms may cross national borders, genetic resources may be obtained from another country, and biological materials or knowledge may be deliberately misused.

These concerns are not governed by one universal biotechnology treaty. Different international agreements address different purposes.

Convention on Biological Diversity

The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) provides the broader international framework for biodiversity conservation, sustainable use and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.

It was opened for signature in 1992 and entered into force on 29 December 1993.

The Cartagena and Nagoya Protocols are supplementary agreements associated with the CBD, but they address different subjects.

Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety

The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety was adopted on 29 January 2000 and entered into force on 11 September 2003.

Its purpose is to contribute to the safe transfer, handling and use of living modified organisms resulting from modern biotechnology that may have adverse effects on biodiversity, while also taking into account risks to human health.

A central concern is the transboundary movement of LMOs, meaning their movement across national boundaries.

Advance informed agreement

The Protocol establishes an advance informed agreement (AIA) procedure for specified intentional transboundary movements of LMOs, particularly the first such movement for intentional introduction into the environment of the importing country.

The procedure is designed to provide the importing country with relevant information before it makes a decision. The exporting country must notify, or require the exporter to notify, the importing country's competent authority in writing before the movement.

The AIA procedure does not apply identically to every movement or use of an LMO. For example, LMOs intended for direct use as food, feed or processing are addressed through separate provisions of the Protocol. Article 11 provides for information sharing through the Biosafety Clearing-House and allows import decisions under domestic rules consistent with the Protocol.

Risk assessment and risk management

Article 15 and Annex III address scientific risk assessment. Article 16 addresses measures for managing identified risks.

The Protocol's approach recognizes that decisions should consider the likely receiving environment, the organism's characteristics, possible adverse effects and the available scientific evidence.

Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing

The Nagoya Protocol was adopted on 29 October 2010 and entered into force on 12 October 2014.

Its central purpose is the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from the utilization of covered genetic resources.

It establishes obligations concerning access, benefit-sharing and compliance, with important roles for prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms under applicable domestic legislation.

Biological Weapons Convention

The Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) addresses a different concern: the prevention and prohibition of biological and toxin weapons.

It opened for signature in 1972 and entered into force in 1975.

Its relevance to biosecurity arises from the need to prevent biological agents and toxins from being developed, acquired or used for prohibited weapons purposes.

Comparison of major international agreements

AgreementKey yearPrincipal concern
Convention on Biological Diversity1992Conservation, sustainable use and fair benefit-sharing
Cartagena Protocol2000Biosafety of living modified organisms and their transboundary movement
Nagoya Protocol2010Access to genetic resources and fair benefit-sharing
Biological Weapons Convention1972Prohibition of biological and toxin weapons

The years in this table identify the adoption year of the CBD and its Protocols and the opening-for-signature year of the BWC. Their entry-into-force dates are different and should not be confused with these dates.

Choosing the relevant framework

When a country considers importing a viable genetically engineered organism for environmental introduction, the Cartagena Protocol provides the relevant international biosafety framework.

When a researcher seeks access to genetic resources covered by access and benefit-sharing requirements, the Nagoya framework becomes relevant.

When the concern is the prohibited development or possession of biological weapons, the BWC is the relevant treaty.

International agreements and domestic regulation

International agreements establish obligations and frameworks for their parties. Domestic legislation and regulatory institutions determine many of the procedures through which those obligations are implemented.

For example, India's environmental biosafety rules and biodiversity legislation address different domestic responsibilities. Approval under one regulatory system does not automatically satisfy every requirement arising under another applicable law.

Prelims focus

  • Cartagena Protocol: adopted on 29 January 2000; effective from 11 September 2003.
  • Nagoya Protocol: adopted on 29 October 2010; effective from 12 October 2014.
  • Cartagena focuses on LMO biosafety; Nagoya focuses on access and benefit-sharing.
  • Biological Weapons Convention: opened for signature in 1972; effective from 1975.
  • AIA under Cartagena means advance informed agreement.
  • Trap: The Cartagena and Nagoya Protocols supplement the CBD but do not govern the same activity.

[Sources: Convention on Biological Diversity, About the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, History and Entry into Force; Cartagena Protocol, Articles 7, 11, 15 and 16, and Annex III; Convention on Biological Diversity, About the Nagoya Protocol, and Articles 5–7; National Biodiversity Authority, FAQs, questions 4–5; United Nations Treaty Collection, Biological Weapons Convention, treaty record; United Nations, Disarmament, Biological Weapons section. Official online sources consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: International Frameworks: Cartagena Protocol, Nagoya Protocol and Biological Weapons Convention

body:
Regulation of biotechnology in India

Biotechnology regulation in India involves different institutions because laboratory research, environmental release, biomedical research ethics and access to biological resources raise different legal and scientific questions.

No single committee performs all these functions. Understanding which institution is responsible for which activity is essential for interpreting questions about biotechnology governance.

Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and Rules, 1989

The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 provides an important legal basis for India's environmental biosafety regulation.

Under this Act, the Government notified the Rules for the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous Micro-organisms, Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells, 1989, commonly called the Rules, 1989.

These Rules establish a regulatory framework for activities involving specified hazardous microorganisms and genetically engineered organisms or cells.

The 6 competent authorities under Rules, 1989

AuthorityFull nameMain responsibility
RDACRecombinant DNA Advisory CommitteeAdvises on biotechnology developments and appropriate biosafety regulations
IBSCInstitutional Biosafety CommitteeOversees implementation of biosafety requirements within an institution
RCGMReview Committee on Genetic ManipulationMonitors safety aspects of relevant ongoing research activities
GEACGenetic Engineering Appraisal CommitteeAppraises specified large-scale activities and proposals for environmental release
SBCCState Biotechnology Coordination CommitteeSupports biosafety compliance and oversight at the state level
DLCDistrict Level CommitteeSupports biosafety oversight and monitoring at the district level

Institutional Biosafety Committee

An IBSC operates at the institutional level in organizations undertaking covered biological research.

Its responsibilities include reviewing relevant proposals, supporting compliance with biosafety requirements and helping ensure that appropriate precautions are applied within the institution.

Where higher-level regulatory review is required, the IBSC reviews the proposal and forwards its recommendation to RCGM or GEAC for the approval required for that activity. Institutional review does not automatically replace authorization by other competent authorities.

Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation

The RCGM functions under the Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Government of India.

It has responsibilities concerning safety-related aspects of ongoing research involving genetically engineered organisms and relevant hazardous microorganisms, within the regulatory framework.

The RCGM and GEAC are separate bodies. The RCGM's research-related role must not be confused with the GEAC's responsibilities concerning environmental release.

Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee

The GEAC functions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC).

Under Rules, 1989, its responsibilities include appraisal of specified large-scale uses of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants from an environmental perspective, as well as proposals involving the environmental release of genetically engineered organisms and products, including experimental field trials.

The committee was originally called the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee. It was renamed the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee through a notification dated 16 July 2010.

GEAC belongs to MoEFCC, while RCGM belongs to DBT. GEAC is associated particularly with environmental appraisal; RCGM is associated with safety oversight of relevant research activities.

State and district biosafety oversight

The State Biotechnology Coordination Committee and District Level Committee form part of the oversight structure established under Rules, 1989.

Their roles concern compliance, monitoring and coordination at state and district levels. These bodies should not be confused with State Biodiversity Boards or local Biodiversity Management Committees, which operate under biodiversity legislation.

Institutions responsible for human research ethics

The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) provides national ethical guidance for biomedical and health research involving human participants.

Institutional Ethics Committees and other appropriately constituted Ethics Committees review proposed research involving human participants, including relevant genetic studies.

Their ethical responsibilities include informed consent, participant welfare, confidentiality, fair selection and reasonable assessment of risks and benefits.

Ethical review and environmental biosafety review are different regulatory functions. Where both apply, satisfying one does not automatically satisfy the other.

India's biodiversity governance structure

The Biological Diversity Act establishes a decentralized institutional system.

National Biodiversity Authority

The National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) is a statutory body established in 2003 under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.

It is headquartered in Chennai, Tamil Nadu.

The NBA performs regulatory, advisory and facilitative functions concerning biological resources, associated traditional knowledge and access and benefit-sharing under the Act.

State Biodiversity Boards

State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) implement relevant biodiversity responsibilities at the state level. Their functions include advising state governments and regulating specified activities involving biological resources according to the applicable legal provisions.

Biodiversity Management Committees

Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) operate at the local level and contribute to biodiversity conservation, sustainable use and documentation of local biological resources and associated traditional knowledge.

They are associated with the preparation and maintenance of People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs), which document local biological diversity and relevant traditional knowledge.

Gujarat-specific institutions and applications

Gujarat Biodiversity Board

The Gujarat Biodiversity Board is Gujarat's State Biodiversity Board under the biodiversity governance framework.

Its headquarters are in Gandhinagar. Gujarat has also notified the Gujarat Biological Diversity Rules, 2010.

The Board and the state's Biodiversity Management Committees have functions connected with biodiversity conservation, documentation, access regulation and benefit-sharing under the applicable framework.

Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre

The Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre (GBRC) is an autonomous research organization established by the Government of Gujarat's Department of Science and Technology in 2017.

It is based in Gandhinagar and undertakes biotechnology research relevant to healthcare, agriculture, environment and other sectors.

Its work includes genomics and other biotechnology applications. The Gujarat government's official institutional information identifies GBRC as a participant in the DBT-supported GenomeIndia initiative and describes its contributions to genomic surveillance and biological research.

These activities illustrate why genetic data governance, biosafety and ethical research practices are relevant in Gujarat's biotechnology ecosystem.

GBRC is a research institution, not the national authority for approving environmental release of genetically engineered organisms. The relevant environmental appraisal function belongs to GEAC under the applicable regulatory framework.

Matching an activity with the appropriate institution

If the main question concerns institutional oversight of covered genetic engineering research, the IBSC and, where applicable, RCGM are relevant.

If the question concerns appraisal of environmental release of a genetically engineered organism, GEAC is central.

If the activity involves human participants in genetic research, an appropriate Ethics Committee and applicable ICMR ethical guidance are relevant.

If the activity concerns access to biological resources, associated traditional knowledge or benefit-sharing, the NBA, relevant SBB and BMC framework becomes important.

Several approvals or reviews may be necessary for a single project, depending on its actual activities and applicable laws.

One-glance revision of the complete subtopic

Prelims focus

  • Environment (Protection) Act: 1986; biotechnology-related regulatory Rules: 1989.
  • GEAC: Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, functioning under MoEFCC.
  • RCGM: Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation, functioning under DBT.
  • NBA: established in 2003 under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002; headquarters at Chennai.
  • Gujarat Biodiversity Board: Gandhinagar; GBRC: established in 2017 and based in Gandhinagar.
  • Trap: GEAC, RCGM, Institutional Ethics Committees and the NBA do not perform interchangeable functions.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, GEAC official website, About GEAC, Functions, and Acts and Rules, including the notification dated 16 July 2010; Department of Biotechnology, Government of India, Guidelines and SOPs for Research on Genetically Engineered Insects, 2023, Annexure I, Mandate and Function of Competent Authorities under Rules, 1989; Department of Biotechnology, Guidelines and Handbook for Institutional Biosafety Committees, 2011, Sections 1–2; National Biodiversity Authority, Introduction, FAQs, questions 10–14, and Gujarat State Biodiversity Rules listing; Government of Gujarat, Department of Science and Technology, Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre, institutional overview, establishment and programmes, official page updated 27 October 2026. Online sources consulted 13 November 2026; institutional and legal descriptions reflect that content cutoff.]
